articles.title: Italian ski great Federica Brignone retires after remarkable injury comeback to win 2 Olympic titles
articles.summary: Federica Brignone's stunning comeback to win two Olympic titles on home Italian snow this year after serious injury turned out to be quite a career swansong. The 36-year-old retired on Wednesday.

image.caption: Italy's Federica Brignone, one of the greatest skiers of this generation, announced her retirement Wednesday in Rome at age 36, citing ongoing pain from her left leg that she broke last year. (Stefano Rellandini/AFP via Getty Images/File)

blocks.text: Federica Brignone's stunning comeback to win two Olympic titles on home Italian snow this year after serious injury turned out to be quite a career swansong. The 36-year-old retired on Wednesday.
'My leg is not fully recovered ... I'm still in too much pain,' says 37-time World Cup winner
Federica Brignone's stunning comeback to win two Olympic titles on home Italian snow this year after serious injury turned out to be quite a career swansong.

One of the greatest skiers of this generation announced her retirement Wednesday in Rome at age 36, citing ongoing pain from her left leg that she broke last year, 10 months before the Milano-Cortina Winter Games.

Brignone's remarkable career of two overall World Cup titles, five Olympic medal — including gold in super-G and giant slalom at Cortina-d'Ampezzo in February — 37 World Cup race wins and five world championship medals will formally end with a farewell race soon.
"I would like to open the starting gate one last time, to say goodbye to this sport that I love so much and to all of you," Brignone wrote in an Instagram post. "I'll let you know where and when."
When Brignone won the second of her overall World Cup titles, the sport's most prized all-around accolade, in 2025 she seemed set to be a home team star at the 2026 Winter Olympics.
Then weeks later she broke multiple bones in her left leg crashing at the season-ending national championships and Olympic ambitions seemed over.
Brignone was unable to walk for three months and her return to ski racing was pushed back deep into the Olympic season.

items: Brignone completes comeback, claims Olympic gold in women's super-G
Italian Olympic women's champion skiers to miss start of World Cup season

blocks.text: Somehow, with just two prep races on the World Cup circuit in January, Brignone got to the Olympics and did not just start but starred.
Now, the injury has proved too much to consider another season on the tiring World Cup circuit where she also was overall champion in 2020.

"After these two days on the snow, I've realized that my leg is not fully recovered yet and that I'm still in too much pain," Brignone wrote Wednesday. "For this reason, I've decided to bring my competitive career to an end.
"It has certainly been a very difficult decision, but despite doing everything I could to get back on track, the severity of my injury simply won't allow me to do so."

articles.title: Federal prosecutors stumble in case over Ontario nuclear plant's worst fish kill
articles.summary: Crown prosecutors have withdrawn and re-laid charges over a massive fish kill in 2025 against Bruce Power, the private operator of Canada's largest nuclear plant, after initially filing the case in…

image.caption: A gizzard shad is held above a fishing net by a provincial conservation worker. The temperature-sensitive species is at the centre of a massive fish kill at Ontario's Bruce Nuclear generating station in 2025. (Upper Thames Conservation Authority)

blocks.text: Canada·New

Crown prosecutors have withdrawn and re-laid charges over a massive fish kill in 2025 against Bruce Power, the private operator of Canada's largest nuclear plant, after initially filing the case in the wrong court.
Bruce Power is due back in court Dec. 9 after the Crown withdrew original 2 charges

Crown prosecutors were forced to start over in their case against the operator of Canada's largest nuclear power plant after initially filing federal Fisheries Act charges in the wrong court over a massive 2025 fish kill.

Bruce Power was charged under Canada's Fisheries Act in October with unlawfully killing fish and violating the conditions of its federal fisheries authorization in connection with a massive fish kill at the plant in 2025.
The case came before a provincial offences court in Walkerton, Ont., on Tuesday, where Crown prosecutors withdrew the charges so they could be brought before the proper court.
The Walkerton court office told CBC News that the new charges are identical to those withdrawn on Tuesday. Bruce Power is now scheduled to appear in criminal court on Dec. 9.
The Public Prosecution Service of Canada, the federal agency responsible for prosecuting offences under federal law, including the Fisheries Act, was unable to immediately comment on Wednesday.
Megan Adams, Bruce Power's director of corporate communications and marketing, declined to comment on the court mix-up, citing the ongoing legal proceedings.
A fish kill of unprecedented scale
Millions of gizzard shad were killed after they overwhelmed the plant's cooling water system in February 2025, forcing Bruce Power to shutdown one reactor and reduce power at another.

As many as 4.95 million gizzard shad died in the incident, with dead fish washing ashore in lakeside communities for days. At the plant, the fish had to be scooped out with a crane and hauled to a landfill.
Dead gizzard shad seen here on a beach on Lake Huron in the spring of 2025 were reported washing up in many localities along the coast. (Submitted by Saugeen Ojibway Nation)

Federal and provincial records obtained by CBC News also revealed the incident "challenged reactor safety" and raised concerns about the growing risks posed by climate change to nuclear power plant cooling systems.
It was the largest fish kill in the plant's history and prompted an investigation by Fisheries and Oceans Canada, culminating in the two federal charges.

Bruce Power has operated the sprawling nuclear generating facility on the shores of Lake Huron, about 200 kilometres northwest of Toronto, since 2001, when it took over operations from provincially owned Ontario Power Generation.
The eight-reactor facility, originally built by Ontario Hydro in the 1970s and '80s, supplies roughly 30 per cent of Ontario's electricity.

articles.title: Poundland collapses into administration, putting 12,000 jobs at risk
articles.summary: US owner Gordon Brothers rejected at least two last-ditch bids for UK budget retailer

blocks.text: Poundland has called in administrators, putting 12,000 jobs at risk in the run-up to Christmas after its owners rejected at least two last-ditch bids for the budget retailer.

Administrators at AlixPartners have been appointed to the retailer, which has 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, by Poundland’s directors. The chain is now expected to be broken up with significant job losses and store closures.
AlixPartners said a sales process “did not identify a viable solvent solution for the business as a whole”.

Poundland would continue to trade with all stores and distribution centres remaining open while administrators pursued “all options including sales of the business and its assets, either in whole or part, from administration”, AlixPartners said.

The retailer’s US owner, Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for a nominal £1 from the European retail group Pepco last year, has been under pressure to accept an offer that would save jobs and protect thousands of the retailer’s suppliers.

The US finance firm said on Wednesday afternoon it had “explored every avenue to secure a sale of the whole company” but that Poundland was “still vulnerable to inflationary pressures or any downturn in sales and margin”.

It said: “Poundland has faced several years of instability. In July 2025, Gordon Brothers supported the company’s restructuring plan – stepping in when no one else was willing to finance the business.”

blocks.caption: The retailer’s US owner, Gordon Brothers, which bought Poundland for a nominal £1 last year, has been under pressure to accept an offer that would save jobs. Photograph: Mike Kemp/In Pictures/Getty

blocks.text: High inflation and heavy competition from budget stores, online specialists and supermarkets have left the 36-year-old retail chain – the UK’s first and biggest nationwide single-price retailer – struggling.

Poundland’s board filed a notice of intention to appoint administrations last month – which was later extended – protecting the retailer from the demands of creditors until 26 November while a solution to its problems was sought.
Just two bidders interested in the whole company remained in talks right up until this week’s deadline.
Martin Property Group, a Northern Ireland family-owned company, which has been working with the existing management, led by Barry Williams, for about two months, remained interested.

It was joined by a last-ditch bid from Germany’s Zachert Private Equity, a fund founded by a former Bloomberg journalist that specialises in acquiring mid-sized companies such as the German photo studio group Studioline, and the US food and drink company Brands Within Reach.
Other bidders for the whole group included the little-known finance group Xyra Group Holdings, and the Irish investment company Innovest, which both fell out of the bidding race over the past week.
AlixPartners said: “We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved – customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues.
“We would encourage anybody interested in acquiring the business in part or as a whole, as well as UK retail operators with open employment opportunities, to contact the administrators.”
after newsletter promotion

Poundland’s board was forced to appoint administrators before Thursday’s deadline as shelves began to empty because the company was running short of funds to restock during its peak Christmas trading period.

Gordon Brothers’ UK director, Mark Newton-Jones, held the latest of several meetings with the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, on Monday, more than a week after giving evidence to the business select committee. MPs called on the government to protect Poundland and other high street stores from “predatory capitalism” and asset-stripping last week.

Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the business select committee, said he had recalled Newton-Jones to give public evidence. He said the committee was seeking assurances that Gordon Brothers or any related party would “not act as administrator, liquidator or in any other insolvency capacity in relation to Poundland”.

Poundland, which was founded with one store in Burton upon Trent in 1990, has endured a rocky history under a string of different owners as it has faced rising costs and heavy competition from chains such as Savers, Home Bargains and B&M, as well as from the big supermarkets.
It is now expected to be broken up with retailers such as Poundstretcher, B&M and The Range taking parcels of stores.
Gordon Brothers rejected an initial management-backed rescue bid financed by Martin Property Group for the discount chain.

The US-based finance company said it could raise more from a breakup of Poundland – selling off stock and parcels of stores to rival retailers – than through the solvent bids. Those bids promised only a small upfront payment for the £30m in shareholder debts that Gordon Brothers took on with its fellow shareholder – Poundland’s former owner Pepco – at the time of buying the chain.
The deals were rejected by Gordon Brothers despite Pepco, which holds £7.5m of the debt, saying it was prepared to wait for repayment in the hope of saving the business.

articles.title: Removal of Premarin highlights difficulty in accessing menopause treatment in Canada
articles.summary: Earlier this month, Pfizer Canada announced it was discontinuing its hormone replacement therapy Premarin in Canada, but not in the U.S., citing “business reasons” — this despite an uptick in demand…

image.caption: Clinicians are raising concerns about access to menopause treatments in the wake of Pfizer ending the sale in Canada of a topical cream commonly prescribed to treat serious menopausal symptoms such as vaginal and vulvar irritation and atrophy, as well as increased risk of recurrent urinary tract inf

blocks.text: Finding menopause treatment that works for your body and doesn’t break the bank can be a long, complicated process — and many Canadians will soon be forced to start that process again.

Earlier this month, Pfizer Canada announced it was discontinuing its menopausal hormone therapy Premarin in Canada, but not in the U.S., citing "business reasons" — this despite an uptick in demand for such products.

Premarin’s topical cream formulation is one of only two vaginal estrogen creams approved by Health Canada and is widely covered under most provincial drug benefits. Now, clinicians are worried about access for their patients — the only other topical cream isn’t currently covered in B.C. and Ontario, Canada’s biggest provinces.

"To have [Premarin] removed actually reduces the access for all of those people — some of the most vulnerable people," said Jessica Bawden, a nurse practitioner and lead clinician in the Women's College Hospital menopause clinic in Toronto.
She noted that some of the symptoms treated by drugs like Premarin, such as the risk of recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs), can have serious consequences if unaddressed.
"A UTI can be deadly, so this can be a preventative medicine to keep people out of hospital," she said. "Menopause is very normal, but suffering is not."

Jessica Bawden works at a menopause clinic in the Women's College Hospital in Toronto, and says she's concerned about access for patients who need to find an alternative for Premarin. (Craig Chivers/CBC)
Premarin comes in a vaginal cream and an oral tablet. The cream has been in short supply for months, but tablets are expected to remain available through mid-2027.

Premarin’s discontinuance comes as other menopausal treatments are becoming harder to find in Canada — a shortage in estradiol transdermal patches across the country is expected to persist into early 2027, according to Health Canada.
Vaginal irritation, pain, risk of recurrent UTIs
Dr. Sheila Wijayasinghe, a family doctor at Unity Health in Toronto, said it was a shock to find out Premarin — "one of the mainstays of our treatment options" — was being discontinued in Canada.

A number of vaginal estrogen products are approved in Canada to treat menopause symptoms, including oral tablets, vaginal suppositories and vaginal rings. The topical cream form of Premarin is commonly prescribed for those experiencing genitourinary syndrome, she said — a cluster of menopausal symptoms including vaginal irritation, vulvar irritation, pain during sexual intercourse and more frequent UTIs.

items: Pfizer ends sale of hormone therapy cream Premarin in Canada
Olympian Clara Hughes was used to pushing her body. But when menopause hit, her body pushed back

blocks.text: "Due to decreasing levels of estrogen, the tissues change. They can become more uncomfortable. We notice symptoms like urinary frequency, incontinence and an increased risk of bladder infections as well," Wijayasinghe said. "We can treat that very effectively with local vaginal estrogen."

Many of the more widely talked about menopause symptoms, like hot flashes and night sweats, get better over time. But genitourinary syndrome can worsen without appropriate treatment, and some form of it will affect the majority of people who go through menopause, she said.
Wijayasinghe also often prescribes Premarin cream to treat recurrent UTIs in seniors, "because it’s a very safe treatment option."
"I don't want to leave my patients without options," Wijayasinghe said. "I don’t want them to have to pay out of pocket if they're low-income … or they don't have private coverage."
Estragyn, made by Searchlight Pharma, is the only other topical cream vaginal estrogen product approved by Health Canada. (Craig Chivers/CBC)
B.C., Alberta expanding coverage options
The only other topical cream alternative approved by Health Canada is Estragyn, which is made by Searchlight Pharma.
It isn't a one-to-one equivalent of Premarin, as it uses the estrogen hormone estrone as its core ingredient, instead of conjugated estrogens.
But for patients who want a cream option — the only vaginal estrogen treatment that provides direct relief for external symptoms affecting the vulva — Estragyn is the sole alternative in Canada.

"[Vaginal suppositories] help more so with symptoms on the inside, but if you're having any symptoms on the outside, then it won't really help much for that," said Alexandra Hanna, a clinical pharmacist in the menopause clinic at Women’s College Hospital.

items: More women are taking testosterone to treat menopause symptoms. Does science support that?

blocks.text: Estragyn costs around $70 a tube if you don’t have public or private coverage, she said. It’s covered by some provincial drug benefits, including Quebec’s and Manitoba’s, but not all.
Regina researcher focused on menopause and mental health
Under the Ontario Drug Benefit, those who are over 65 can access medications covered by OHIP; Premarin was one of those drugs. But Estragyn isn’t covered in Ontario.

When asked by CBC News if Ontario would consider adding Estragyn to the Ontario Drug Benefit, the province's Ministry of Health shared a list of three alternative vaginal estrogen products that Ontario already covers — none of which were topical creams.
Some provinces, however, are stepping up to expand coverage.

A spokesperson for Alberta’s health ministry said it has added Estragyn "as a temporary benefit" in response to Pfizer’s discontinuation of Premarin, and is working with the manufacturer to explore permanent coverage.

B.C.’s Ministry of Health, which covers Premarin cream through the National PharmaCare Plan, told CBC News it is "actively reviewing Estragyn as the replacement cream option following the discontinuation of Premarin."

Alexandra Hanna, a clinical pharmacist in the menopause clinic at Toronto's Women’s College Hospital, says patients should plan next steps with their doctors now instead of waiting for their Premarin supply to run out, to avoid gaps in their care. (Craig Chivers/CBC News)
Hanna hopes Ontario expands its coverage to include Estragyn, noting that many patients have been frustrated by Premarin’s discontinuation.
"For a lot of them, it takes a lot of trial and error to find something that works for them," she said.

There’s no generic form of Premarin cream, and switching to any new medication can be tough on the body. She advised that patients currently taking Premarin start discussing alternatives with their doctors now, instead of waiting.
Why did Pfizer discontinue the drug if demand is increasing?

It’s not uncommon for older drugs to be taken off the market, but Pfizer’s decision to discontinue Premarin in Canada, but not the U.S., has raised eyebrows, especially since its active ingredient — conjugated equine estrogens from pregnant mare urine — is produced in Brandon, Man.

Pfizer Canada told CBC News the decision reflected "a broader assessment of the long-term commercial sustainability" of supplying Premarin to Canada, adding they looked at "manufacturing and supply costs, the pricing and reimbursement environment, and the ability to maintain sustainable supply over the longer term."

“[Premarin] is a little bit more challenging than typical drugs to produce,” said Mina Tadrous, associate professor at the Lesley Dan Faculty of Pharmacy at the University of Toronto. “So there could be some truth in the higher cost and what those margins look like for them.”
As menopause products boom, many don't live up to the hype

He noted that global demand is up for menopause products amid increasing awareness in recent years. In the U.S. alone, monthly dispensing of menopause hormone therapy for women aged 40-74 years increased from two million in 2023 to 4.9 million by June 2026, a 141 per cent increase, according to a recent study published in JAMA.
This could have been a factor in Pfizer’s decision to withdraw it from the Canadian market despite increased demand here, too, Tadrous said.

"We've been for the last three years seeing a number of shortages for menopause-related therapies," Tadrous said. In the long term, the supply chain could catch up as companies enter to capitalize on demand, "but in the short term, you get this pain when you have these sudden increases in demand."

Pharmaceutical experts previously warned that a deal U.S. President Donald Trump made with pharmaceutical companies in September to lower drug prices in the U.S. could also impact Canada, suggesting companies might delay launching new drugs here to avoid creating a lower price comparison that could pull U.S. prices down further.
Trump’s push to cut pharma costs could drive up drug prices in Canada

In a blog post last Thursday, Canadian obstetrician-gynecologist Dr. Jen Gunter noted that a tube of Premarin cream in the U.S. sells for roughly $400-$500 US, 10 times more than what it costs in Canada.

items: What Trump's 'most favoured nation' drug pricing policy might mean for Canadians

blocks.text: Tadrous said it's tough to make the connection between the Premarin discontinuation and Trump's new most-favoured-nation (MFN) drug pricing, in part because of its age on the market.
But when products get pulled, Canada needs to find ways to stop patients from bearing the brunt, he said.
"I think what we need to do is start being more proactive. So when we know a drug is changing like this, can we go and find another source for it? Can we invest locally?" he said.
"How do we empower health-care providers and patients to be able to navigate this a little bit more easily?"

articles.title: Edmonton to host 2028 Grey Cup
articles.summary: The Edmonton Elks and the Canadian Football League announced that the 2028 Grey Cup will be held in Edmonton. The last time Commonwealth Stadium hosted a Grey Cup was in 2018, when the Calgary…

image.caption: A file photo of Commonwealth Stadium in Edmonton, on Tuesday, June 1, 2021. (Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton·Breaking

The Edmonton Elks and the Canadian Football League announced that the 2028 Grey Cup will be held in Edmonton. The last time Commonwealth Stadium hosted a Grey Cup was in 2018, when the Calgary Stampeders beat the Ottawa Redblacks 27-16.
Commonwealth Stadium last hosted the Grey Cup in 2018
The 2028 Grey Cup is coming to Edmonton.
The Edmonton Elks, the winners of this year's championship, and the Canadian Football League made the announcement Wednesday in Edmonton.
The 115th Grey Cup game will be played at Commonwealth Stadium.
The last time Commonwealth Stadium hosted the Grey Cup was in 2018, when the Calgary Stampeders beat the Ottawa Redblacks 27-16.

While Edmonton has won 15 Grey Cups, none of them have been won at Commonwealth Stadium. Their closest opportunity was in 2002, when the team lost 25-16 to the Montreal Alouettes in front of a spillover crowd of 62,531.
The announcement comes just over a week after the Elks won the 113th Grey Cup game in Calgary, securing the club's 15th championship in franchise history and its first Grey Cup win in 11 years.
Saskatchewan is set to host the 2027 Grey Cup game at Mosaic Stadium in Regina.

articles.title: Kilmar Ábrego García, target of Trump’s immigration crackdown, lands in Spain after ‘leaving happy’
articles.summary:
Ábrego García chose to depart from US after previously being deported to El Salvador due to ‘administrative error’

Kilmar Ábrego García, the Salvadoran national whose mistaken deportation…
articles.byline: Ashifa Kassam in Madrid and Uwa Ede-Osifo

blocks.text: Kilmar Ábrego García, the Salvadoran national whose mistaken deportation turned him into a symbol of Donald Trump’s mass deportation efforts, has landed in Spain.

Ábrego García arrived in Madrid on Wednesday after leaving the United States of his own volition. Prior to his departure, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents met him at the airport and removed his ankle monitor, according to We Are CASA, a Maryland-based advocacy group.
The interaction, the group noted, was “a powerful symbol that ends a chapter marked by illegal deportation, imprisonment, abuse at Cecot, retaliatory prosecution, and government surveillance”.
As he made his way through the Madrid airport, Ábrego García did not speak to reporters, instead raising his fist in the air as he climbed into a waiting van.
In a statement provided by We Are CASA, he described his departure from the US as proof that justice was still capable of prevailing over the most powerful government in the world.

“In this case, despite everything they tried to say, every obstacle they put in my way, and every attempt to shame me, justice prevailed under this administration in a way that many people never thought was possible,” he said. “I am leaving happy. I am leaving with my freedom.”
Ábrego García became a lightning rod in the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in 2025 after he was deported to El Salvador in what an official later called an “administrative error”.
The 31-year-old had been living in the US since 2019, after a judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador due to the dangers posed by a gang that had threatened his family.
Married to an American woman, the Maryland resident was sent to Cecot, a notorious anti-terrorism mega-prison, in violation of the US immigration judge’s 2019 order.

Amid public outcry, he was returned to the US after a decision by the supreme court. Since then, Ábrego García has been fighting government efforts to deport him for a second time to a series of African countries proposed by Department of Homeland Security officials.
On Wednesday, his lawyer, Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, said that the Trump administration had wanted to deport Ábrego García “handcuffed, on an ICE flight bound for Liberia” on Tuesday.

“And what happened? He walked out a free man, without any restrictions, without shackles on his feet. He left for the country of his choosing, and he did so on a commercial flight, alongside everyone else,” Sandoval-Moshenberg added, describing it as “a victory”.

The Washington Post reported earlier this week that Ábrego García had negotiated a deal with federal authorities to depart the US voluntarily in order to avoid being forcibly removed. The US Department of Homeland Security said Tuesday that Ábrego García had “self-deported” to Spain.

Sandoval-Moshenberg described Ábrego García’s departure from the US as temporary. “Mr Ábrego García has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a US citizen spouse and the father of a US citizen child,” he said. “We don’t expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritise reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland.”

On Wednesday, Ábrego García’s lawyer, Chris Newman, said his client had landed in Spain as a tourist. “I can confirm that he’s coming here with the intention of staying for just a few days and that he already has tickets, one could say, for his next appointment,” he told Spanish media.

His departure this week was celebrated by many who had sought to push back against the Trump administration’s pursuit of Ábrego García. “A year and a half ago, the Trump Admin wanted to leave Kilmar to rot in a Salvadoran gulag,” said Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland senator who visited Abrego Garcia at Cecot, in a statement.
“Today, he is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man – unharmed and with dignity.”

articles.title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
articles.summary: All three main US indexes were down in early trading, with the tech-dominated Nasdaq down almost 4%.

blocks.text: Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.
All three main US stock market indices were down, with the tech-dominated Nasdaq shedding almost 4%.
The declines come amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment which has rattled investors in recent weeks.
Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and SpaceX, Micrsoft and Meta were also down.
The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.

The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs, but share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry.
The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia boss Jensen Huang after revelations of his extra marital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.
Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.
Investors have taken fright at Democrat gains in the US midterm elections, with many having campaigned for tougher regulation of AI firms and even a moratorium on the development of new data centres.
Questions also remain about whether the huge sums being invested in AI will eventually pay off.

"It seems that these companies are trying to one-up each other on the amount of money that they're spending but you have to show that it's worth it, and that's where Wall Street is saying I don't know," said Todd Schoenberger, chief investment officer at CrossCheck Management.

Despite concerns, investment in AI is expected to exceed $1 trillion in 2026, according to investment bank Goldman Sachs, which said the technology will remain the "dominant driver of business investment growth" next year.
Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased.
Shares in Anthropic continued to trade below the $83 they debuted at last week, while Amazon shares fell by more than 5%.
The declines come ahead of the US stock market closing for Thanksgiving on Thursday before opening for a shortened session on Friday.

articles.title: €561 Billion and Still Not Enough: Germany's 2027 Budget Exposes a Coalition on the Brink
articles.summary: The budget for 2027 has reached new highs, and pension funds, defense spending and a weak economy are increasing the pressure. At the same time, tensions are mounting within the government.

image.caption: The Bundestag is debating the 2027 federal budget this weekImage: Michael Kappeler/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: At first glance, everything seems to be business as usual. Lawmakers in the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, are holding four days of final debates on how much money the federal government may spend in the coming year, and on what. These follow a familiar pattern: The government pats itself on the back, while the opposition voices criticism. But anyone listening more closely will notice that there are doubts even in the ranks of the coalition parties, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), their Bavarian allies, the Christian Social Union (CSU), and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).

"As a country, we are in a difficult situation geopolitically, technologically, and demographically, and next year's budget is an accurate reflection of that," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) acknowledged on Wednesday in the Bundestag.

"If we don't change course, in a few years we'll find ourselves in a situation where all federal revenue will have to be spent on social programs, interest payments, and defense," he reflected on Wednesday during a four-hour debate focused on government policy as a whole, rather than the individual budgets of the ministries.
€200 billion in new borrowing: Germany's not so frugal budget

This government has now been in office for about 20 months. Back in early 2025, expectations were enormous. Merz had promised to bring the budget back in line with the debt brake enshrined in the constitution, which stipulates that the government can spend only as much as it collects.

Yet for 2027, spending — at just under €561 billion ($614 billion) — will be higher than ever before, and tax revenues are nowhere near sufficient to cover this, meaning Germany is looking at a record debt totaling €210 billion.

The largest opposition party, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) calculated that the government will incur €401,000 in new debt every minute next year. In the Bundestag, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla called it a "debt orgy" that will paralyze the country. Merz will "go down in history as the chancellor who led Germany to bankruptcy," he exclaimed.
Record spending and record debt

Germany's debt has only ever been higher in the COVID-19 pandemic. The current pressures are obvious: The economy is struggling, the population aging, and Russia's war against Ukraine is about to enter its sixth year.
Merz accused of 'blackmail' over Ukraine funding

The defense budget is now by far the highest in the history of the Federal Republic, with €109 billion allocated for 2027, an increase of €27 billion on last year. Added to this is the multi-year, debt-financed special military fund, intended to modernize the armed forces, bringing the total defense budget to €139 billion.
Defense spending rises to historic levels

The AfD and the socialist Left Party have sharply criticized this. Left Party parliamentary leader Heidi Reichinnek accused the government of pursuing "militarization and boundless rearmament on the one hand, and brutal social cuts and an orgy of budget cuts on the other."

The AfD's Chrupalla said that the temporary reduction in the electricity tax, pushed through at the last minute, would save the average family a mere €100 a year, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy "walks out of the chancellery here in Berlin with a check for €200 million after just one afternoon." "Whose chancellor are you, Mr. Merz?" he asked.

The opposition Greens did not agree. While they also criticized the budget as "unserious," Green Party Bundestag member Britta Haßelmann described the AfD's stance on Ukraine as shameful. She rejected the idea that money was being wasted on Ukraine, saying that supporting Ukraine bolstered security for Germany and Europe.
Aid to Ukraine: Still a central controversy

The chancellor shares this view. "You can't say it often enough, either to the far right or the far left: Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than just Ukraine," Merz said. Russia is escalating tensions in the Baltic region, in Poland, in the Black Sea, and in space. Moscow is also seeking escalation in Germany, even at the cost of lives. "That is why we must show Russia its limits," he said.

But it is becoming increasingly difficult for the government to justify the high spending on Ukraine. Germany's pension and health care costs are only getting bigger: By far the largest single budget item is that of the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is growing to over €200 billion, even with cuts to unemployment benefits.
Social spending growing faster than revenue

Work is currently underway on a reform of the pension system — something that many see as urgent, as the workforce born in the 1960s, when more than a million children were born in Germany every year, is on brink of retiring. Birth rates nearly halved by the mid-1970s and declined even further afterward. For now, so-called "boomers" still make up one-third of the current workforce — but soon they will be drawing pensions.

Even now, Germany's pensions cannot be financed solely with contributions on wages and salaries. In 2025, just over €420 billion in pensions were paid out, with the government contributing €127 billion of that amount. By 2027, the government aims to save €3 billion on this figure, which is likely to further increase pension contributions.
Pension reform becomes a test for the coalition

The coalition parties are stuck in a row over how to reform the pension system. Chancellor Merz insisted in the Bundestag that the coalition was solving the country's fundamental problems, but he warned that in future, tax revenues "will no longer be enough to afford everything we have become all too accustomed to," he said. "All of us here will have to give up some of the ideas we cherish."

The SPD, on the other hand, is counting on increasing federal revenue. SPD parliamentary leader Matthias Miersch emphasized in the Bundestag that large fortunes and inheritances must contribute more to "public costs."

That, he said, must also apply to large companies. Currently, heirs to family-owned businesses often pay significantly less in taxes than heirs to real estate or financial assets, because they can be exempted from inheritance tax if they continue to run the business. This is intended to protect them from having to pay taxes in the event of a breakup or sale of the company.
SPD calls for higher taxes on fortunes

According to Miersch, the government must now think about taxing the wealthy more. "For us, this issue is by no means off the table; on the contrary, we are putting it on the agenda," he said. The government's revenue situation is "an issue we need to discuss."

All in all, the outlook for 2027 is strained — and not just financially. The political differences between the CDU/CSU and the SPD are likely to make working together even more difficult. Conflict is inevitable, especially with several state elections scheduled for the spring.

The chancellor knows this and tried to appear confident that better collaboration was possible: "We must seek compromise in our joint decision-making, represented by these — admittedly quite different — coalition partners," he said.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Israeli strike kills 2 senior Hamas officials
articles.summary: The second strike left four people dead, including two children. Witnesses say they were given no prior warning and the explosion happened in the middle of the night, while everyone was sleeping.

image.caption: Mourners carry the bodies of Muhammad Abu al-Ouf, a Hamas internal security officer, and his family, during their funeral in Gaza City. They were killed in an Israeli strike. (Jehad Alshrafi/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New
The second strike left four people dead, including two children. Witnesses say they were given no prior warning and the explosion happened in the middle of the night, while everyone was sleeping.
Israel says it was targeting Hamas officials in charge of security in northern Gaza

It was a chaotic scene in the Al Shati refugee camp in Gaza City after an Israeli strike hit an apartment building, leaving four dead and multiple injuries. It shattered the facade and left furniture and toys strewn on the ground.
Witnesses say multiple people were sheltering nearby and the strike came with no prior notice.

The Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said they were targeting a senior Hamas security official who was sheltering in the building with his wife and two children. Mohammad Abuelouf was a Hamas colonel who headed the militant’s internal security service in northern Gaza.
It was the second senior Hamas security official killed in the last 24 hours. Yesterday afternoon, IDF targeted Naim Abu Nahal in a displacement camp in Gaza City — he was also the head of security.
A Palestinian man inspects an apartment destroyed in an Israeli strike in Gaza City. (Jehad Alshrafi/The Associated Press)

IDF strikes have continued throughout the ceasefire as Israel insists it will go after Hamas officials until they lay down their arms. Peace talks have not moved beyond the first phase announced last October and both sides blame the other for the lack of progress.
Mahmoud Bakr, 33, was sheltering near the site of the strike when the explosion happened. He says there’s no safety in Gaza.
"This is what you call a ceasefire?" he told CBC freelance videographer Mohamed El Saife. "If, while we’re sleeping bombs fall on us, then where is the ceasefire?"

The Israeli military confirmed it had killed Abuelouf, whom it described as a ​significant figure who "served as a key source of expertise in efforts to restrict the IDF’s ⁠counterterrorism operations in the Gaza Strip."

Despite a year-old ceasefire, Israel has continued to carry out attacks that it ​says target Hamas but have also killed many civilians. The broader ceasefire plan, backed by U.S. President Donald Trump, ​has not halted the violence or secured Hamas's disarmament.
Palestinian children look at an apartment destroyed in an Israeli strike in Gaza City. (Jehad Alshrafi/The Associated Press)

Medics said Wednesday's airstrike had ripped through Abuelouf's apartment in the Beach refugee camp in western Gaza City, near the coast. Later in the morning, another Israeli airstrike hit Gaza City's northern Karama neighbourhood, killing one person, medics said.

The Israeli military said Abuelouf had helped, during the war and more recently, to advance attacks ​against Israeli forces and civilians and had worked to restore the capabilities of Hamas in violation of the 2025 ceasefire deal.

In a statement posted to Telegram, Hamas called the attack a "massacre." They said the latest targeting of Abuelouf "constitutes a flagrant violation of international and humanitarian laws, and reflects its determination to press ahead with its plans of genocide."
On Tuesday, after the military killed Naeem Abu Nahel, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said there was no escape for Hamas from his country's "long reach."
Israel controls two-thirds of Gaza
At least 1,600 Palestinians and five Israeli soldiers have been killed since the ceasefire was struck ​in October 2025, according to respective Palestinian and Israeli tallies.
Israeli troops now control around ​two-thirds of Gaza, ⁠up from more than half at the time of the ceasefire, with Hamas controlling a sliver of territory along Gaza's coast.

items: Senior Hamas commander who helped oversee Oct. 7 attack killed in Israeli strike in Gaza
Camps destroyed in 2 Israeli military strikes on Gaza City

blocks.text: Hamas's internal security service, which Abu Nahel ran ​and in which Abuelouf was ​a senior official, counters ⁠Palestinians suspected of collaboration with Israel's secret service and gathers information about its plans.

Gaza’s Board of Peace delivered an update on its progress to the United Nations Security Council earlier this month, warning diplomats of a collapse of the fragile agreement if steps are not taken for full implementation.
The BoP report calls on both Israel and Hamas to uphold the commitments made last year under the agreement and urges the UN’s most powerful body to lend its support to the execution of its plan.
Palestinians inspect the wreckage of a car hit by an Israeli strike in Gaza City. (Jehad Alshrafi/The Associated Press)

"The distance between what has been agreed and what is happening on the ground nonetheless remains the principal risk to the process," says the report, a copy of which was obtained by The Associated Press.

It is the latest admonishment from the board in recent weeks, as deadly Israeli strikes and the continued blocking of humanitarian aid to Gaza have caused widespread hardship to the civilian population, which the board says is set to face "another winter in tents and rubble."

Israel says it has allowed 91,000 tents into Gaza over the past three months, a quantity far short of the number the UN says is needed, since much of the territory’s population of almost two million rely on them for shelter and they do not last long. It says it has 100,000 more tents waiting to be allowed into Gaza.

"Restrictions imposed by Israel on the entry of supplies and equipment, compounded by funding shortfalls, continued to impede preparedness and response efforts," the report said, calling for immediate "scaled-up entry of shelter and winterization materials" and approvals for pumps, generators and heavy machinery.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Yasmine Hassan is a producer in CBC's Ottawa bureau. From there, she covers developments inside Gaza and the West Bank related to the Israel-Hamas war. If you have a story idea, send news tips in English or Arabic to yasmine.hassan@cbc.ca.
With files from Reuters and The Associated Press

articles.title: Lacson alleges House push to remove 'Anti-Epal' clause from 2027 budget
articles.summary: Senator Panfilo Lacson on Wednesday floated that certain members of the House of Representatives are seeking to have the provision barring politicians from the distribution of financial assistance…

blocks.text: Published November 26, 2026 12:02am

Senator Panfilo Lacson on Wednesday floated that certain members of the House of Representatives are seeking to have the provision barring politicians from the distribution of financial assistance removed from the 2027 national budget.

This was raised amid the Senate plenary deliberations on the proposed P253.34 billion budget of the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) and its attached agencies for the next fiscal year.
During the session, Lacson asked budget sponsor Senator Risa Hontiveros if the DSWD has full control over the disbursement of the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS).
Hontiveros, who was taking answers from DSWD Secretary Rex Gatchalian, said the agency is maintaining that it has full control over the decision-making in the AICS program.
“I’m sorry, but I don’t believe that. That's why some congressmen are pushing for the AICS,” Lacson said.
“Actually, meron tayong parang I think forthcoming na bicam. Ito ‘yung sa Bawal Epal, gusto nila tanggalin ‘yung provision eh, sa Bawal Epal. They want to retain that, na merong epal,” he added.

(Actually, I believe there’s a bicameral conference coming up. This is regarding the Anti-Epal provision. They want to remove that provision. They want to retain that there is indeed an epal among them.)

The word “epal” is Filipino slang for someone who wants attention or wants to be noticed, especially in a way that’s inappropriate or self-serving. In politics, it usually refers to officials who take credit for government projects to boost their public image or electoral appeal.
In the 2026 General Appropriations Act (GAA), a so-called "anti-epal" special provision was included, preventing politicians from using government programs, projects, or funds to promote themselves.
Guarantee letters

During the budget deliberations, Lacson likewise questioned a provision in the House version of the 2027 budget bill which he said would allow the settlement of unpaid claims from guarantee letters issued in 2024.
He pointed out that the P34.269 billion allocation for the AICS program under the 2024 GAA had already been fully obligated.
“Ang sinasabi po rito, ‘yung guarantee letters issued in 2024, babayaran sa GAA in 2027. Parang nag-issue ng tseke na walang pondo ng 2024. Popondohan ng GAA ng 2027,” Lacson said.

(It seems that guarantee letters issued in 2024 will be paid for through the GAA in 2027. It’s like saying checks were issued in 2024 without any funds to back them. The 2027 GAA will be the one to pay for it.)

Lacson was referring to Special Provision No. 2 in the House General Appropriations Bill (HGAB), where the DSWD’s proposed budget provides for a “Protective Services Program for Individuals and Families in Difficult Circumstances.”

Under the special provision, the amount appropriated for such “shall likewise be used for the payment of arrears to accredited and/or partner service providers arising from the issuance of guarantee letter in fiscal year 2024, subject to the availability of funds and compliance with applicable budgeting, accounting, and auditing laws, rules and regulations.”
Hontiveros admitted that such information was shocking, but said there were service providers that belatedly filed money claims and submitted supporting documents.
“Kaya ngayon lamang ni-request and special provision na ito sa fiscal year 2027,” she said.
(That’s why this special provision is being requested only now for fiscal year 2027.) —LDF, GMA News
