articles.title: Senate realigns P19.8B from MAP, AICS to boost PhilHealth
articles.summary: Senator JV Ejercito says the realigned funds would go directly to hospitals to support the implementation of the Zero Balance Billing program

blocks.text: GAB. Senator JV Ejercito, chairperson of the committee on finance, sponsors the proposed 2027 General Appropriations Act on November 23, 2026, at the Senate of the Philippines, Pasay City.
Senate Facebook
Senator JV Ejercito says the realigned funds would go directly to hospitals to support the implementation of the Zero Balance Billing program

items: The Philippine Senate has realigned nearly P20 billion from various government assistance programs to increase funding for PhilHealth in the proposed 2027 national budget.
Senator JV Ejercito stated that the realignment would raise PhilHealth's allocation from P73 billion to P94.2 billion, with a target to eventually reach P100 billion despite fiscal constraints.
Concerns about potential duplicate funding for infrastructure projects were acknowledged, with Ejercito urging budget watchdogs to help identify any irregularities in the budget.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Senate has realigned nearly P20 billion from government assistance programs, including the Medical Assistance Program (MAP) and the Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations (AICS), to augment funding for the Philippine Health Insurance Corporation (PhilHealth) under the proposed 2027 national budget.

Senator JV Ejercito, chairperson of the Senate finance committee, said on Wednesday, November 25, that the P19.8-billion realignment would help increase PhilHealth’s allocation from P73 billion in the House version of the General Appropriations Bill (GAB) to P94.2 billion in the Senate version of the budget measure.
PhilHealth subsidies in the national budget cover the premium contributions of vulnerable sectors that cannot afford to pay their own health insurance premiums.

“Our target is to increase PhilHealth subsidy to P100 billion but we have a tight fiscal space. Hopefully, we can reach our target so PhilHealth can have better subsidies,” Ejercito told reporters in a mix of English and Filipino.
Of the P19.8 billion, P9.9 billion was realigned from MAP funds and another P9.9 billion from AICS.

Ejercito said the funds would go directly to hospitals to support the implementation of the Zero Balance Billing (ZBB) program. This includes P7.6 billion for Department of Health (DOH) hospitals, P2 billion for legacy hospitals, and P1 billion for local government unit (LGU) hospitals.

The Senate also provided an additional P5.49 billion for the Hospital Facilities Enhancement Program (HFEP), P1.099 billion for health promotion, P1.599 billion for immunization programs, and P736 million for the Sulu Transition Program.

Ejercito also addressed concerns raised by Senator Panfilo “Ping” Lacson over possible duplicate funding for infrastructure projects, including multi-purpose buildings (MPBs), under the proposed 2027 national budget.

“If we saw red flags, including double entries in the GAB, definitely, we’ll remove that. But of course, it is not humanly possible to check everything at once. That’s thousands of entries, so we need to check it slowly,” Ejercito said.

He acknowledged that some questionable entries might have escaped the committee’s scrutiny, but said this was not intentional. He also called on budget watchdogs to help identify possible irregularities.

“If some entries have been let out of our sight, that’s not intentional. So we’re seeking everyone’s help, including budget watchdogs, to tell us if they observe some red flags. If we found that it has basis, we’ll definitely remove the items,” Ejercito added.

The Senate began plenary deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for fiscal year 2027 on Monday, November 23. Lacson, ahead of the deliberations, flagged alleged double and triple appropriations for some flood control projects in the GAB, saying some of them had already received funding in previous years. – Rappler.com

articles.title: In Afghanistan, no female doctor often means no treatment for women
articles.summary: Millions of women in Afghanistan, particularly pregnant women, are suffering under Taliban restrictions and are increasingly losing access to life-saving medical care.

image.caption: The UN has been training women as midwives to work in local communities [FILE 2023]Image: Ali Khara/REUTERS

blocks.text: In many parts of Taliban-ruled Afghanistan, male doctors are no longer allowed to treat women. The consequences have been highlighted in a recent United Nations report, which offers disturbing insight into the harsh reality many women face.
In one case, a woman from Kunar province described how she suffered several miscarriages without being able to access medical care.
Her case highlights the increasing number of pregnant women who urgently need medical assistance and are unable to receive it because of restrictions imposed by the Taliban.
And overall, women in Afghanistan are increasingly losing access to essential healthcare. This is due both to the Taliban's restrictions and to cuts in international aid funding.
Taliban remove women from public life in Afghanistan
"If a pregnant woman dies because male doctors are not allowed to treat her, her husband can marry another, younger woman. That is how the Taliban think," said 28-year-old Tamana Zaryab Paryani.
Paryani is an Afghan women's rights activist and one of the best-known voices of resistance against the Taliban.
'Don't send us back': Afghan women in India fear deportation

A trained lawyer, she worked as a newspaper journalist before the Taliban returned to power. Following their takeover in August 2021, she took part in protests against restrictions on the rights of women and girls. In January 2022, she was detained by the Taliban in Kabul alongside her sisters. After her release, she managed to reach Europe.

Since then, she has continued to advocate internationally for the rights of Afghan women. At the end of October, she addressed the UN Security Council, describing the repression of women in Afghanistan and urging the international community not to normalise their systematic disenfranchisement.
"This is gender apartheid. We expect the international community to recognise it and stand with the women of Afghanistan," Paryani told DW.

Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have issued more than 100 decrees severely restricting the lives of women and girls. Girls are barred from secondary education, while women are denied access to universities. Women's opportunities to work outside the home are also severely restricted.
In Afghanistan, girls study in secret to skirt Taliban ban

The UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA), which monitors and regularly documents the human rights situation in the country, reported in September 2025 that inspectors from the Taliban's Ministry for the Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice were further restricting women's access to healthcare through the enforcement of regulations and decrees.

According to the UN, around 2.6 million girls are excluded from secondary education. This is likely to lead to more girls being married off at an early age and to an increase in maternal mortality, UN Women warns.
Afghanistan has a population of around 45 million. With a median age of approximately 17, it has one of the youngest populations in the world. Around 42% of its population is under the age of 15.
The world's 'worst women's rights crisis'

"What is happening in Afghanistan goes beyond gender-based persecution, as already defined under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court," Haroon Mutasem, professor of International Criminal Law at the American University of Afghanistan and research fellow at Berlin's Humboldt University, told DW.
The Afghan legal scholar examines how the systematic oppression of women in Afghanistan can be classified and prosecuted under international law.

"This is not just about individual acts of persecution, but about an institutionalised system of oppression and domination of one gender group by another. They have established a system that considers women as secondary and defines a life for them as raising kids, working at home, and also actually satisfying the sexual desires of their men."

Mutasem argues that a failure to respond to the systematic oppression of Afghan women could undermine the universal validity of human and women's rights. He warns that other authoritarian regimes and extremist movements could adopt similar practices.
According to UN estimates, in 2027 more than 4 million children under the age of five, as well as around 1.27 million pregnant and breastfeeding women, will require treatment for acute malnutrition.

Susan Ferguson, the UN's Special Representative in Afghanistan, described the situation in her latest report as "the world's worst women's rights crisis." Afghan women, she said, are now "fighting for their very survival."
Cuts in aid funding have forced humanitarian organisations to make "impossible decisions about which women and girls can receive support and which have to be turned away," Ferguson said.
Exiled Afghanistan envoy still advocating for women's rights
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Veteran Nigerian Nollywood actor Pete Edochie dies aged 79
articles.summary: Odochie rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.

blocks.text: Veteran Nigerian actor Pete Edochie, one of Africa's most celebrated film stars, has died at the age of 79, his family has announced.

Known for his deep voice, commanding screen presence and memorable use of African proverbs, Edochie became a household name across Africa, often portraying powerful traditional rulers, wealthy businessmen and family patriarchs.
In a statement, his family said Edochie died in the early hours of Wednesday in the south-eastern Nigerian city of Enugu following a prolonged battle with prostate cancer.
Tributes are pouring in from fans and fellow actors, remembering him as a Nollywood legend who helped shape Nigeria's film industry.

Edochie began his career as a broadcaster in 1967 before turning to acting. He rose to prominence in 1987 after starring in a television adaptation of Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart.

His portrayal of Okonkwo, the proud but troubled Igbo warrior in Chinua Achebe's acclaimed novel Things Fall Apart, earned him international recognition helping establish him as one of Nigeria's most respected actors.
The television series depicted the struggles of an African community as British colonial rule and Christianity began to transform its traditional way of life.
He went on to become one of the most recognisable faces of Nollywood, Nigeria's film industry, which has since grown into one of the world's largest film industries.
Over a career spanning several decades, he appeared in numerous films, including Igodo, Rituals, Billionaire's Club and the 2018 romantic comedy Lionheart.
His contribution to the arts was recognised in 2003 when he received one of Nigeria's national honours, the Member of the Order of the Niger (MON).
He also received several other accolades during his career, including the Industry Merit Award at the Africa Magic Viewers' Choice Awards.
In recent years, his distinctive facial expressions, witty remarks and memorable scenes from his films found a new generation of admirers through viral social media memes.

"As we mourn this painful loss, we pray that Almighty God grants his gentle soul eternal rest and gives the entire family the fortitude to bear this irreparable loss," a statement shared on Instagram by his son Leo said.
Enugu State Governor Peter Mbah said Edochie's death was a huge loss to Nigeria, praising the actor for introducing international audiences to Igbo traditions and inspiring younger performers.
"Pete Edochie was more than an accomplished actor, he was an institution," Mbah said.
The Actors Guild of Nigeria (AGN) president, Abubakar Yakubu, described Edochie as a "father figure" in the entertainment industry, saying his influence would be felt for generations to come.
Edochie had spoken publicly about his deteriorating health during a visit to Ghana in October, saying he was struggling to walk and experiencing swelling in parts of his body.
He is survived by his wife, Josephine, and their six children, including fellow Nollywood actors Yul and Linc Edochie.

articles.title: DAR assures P600-M quick response fund amid El Niño threat
articles.summary: The Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR) said it has a P600-million quick response fund (QRF) ready to cushion agrarian reform beneficiaries against the looming effects of Super El Niño.

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 8:20pm
The Department of Agrarian Reform (DAR) said it has a P600-million quick response fund (QRF) ready to cushion agrarian reform beneficiaries against the looming effects of Super El Niño.
Budget sponsor Senator Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan said this during the Senate plenary deliberations into the proposed P16.121 billion budget of the DAR for fiscal year 2027.

“Dati walang quick response fund ang DAR. Naglaan tayo this year ng P600 million in anticipation of the impact of El Niño. Kaya meron silang quick response fund para matutukan ‘yung magiging impact ng El Niño lalo na sa ating mga magsasaka that form part of the agrarian reform beneficiaries and the communities,” he said.

(Previously, the DAR did not have a quick response fund. This year, we allocated P600 million in anticipation of the impact of El Niño. This provides them with a quick response fund to address the effects of El Niño, particularly for our farmers, that form part of the agrarian reform beneficiaries and the communities.)
Pangilinan gave the update after Senator Bong Go asked about the preparations of DAR to mitigate the expected effects of El Niño on agrarian reform beneficiaries (ARBs).

“With the threat of El Niño, we are concerned about its potential adverse effects on our agricultural sector, particularly on our agrarian reform beneficiaries whose livelihood heavily depends on farming,” Go said.

“Hindi po sapat na mabigyan lang ng sariling lupa ang ating mga magsasaka. Kailangan ding tiyakin natin na mayroon silang sapat na suporta lalo na sa panahon ng kalamidad at matinding tagtuyot,” he added.
(It’s not enough to simply provide our farmers with their own land. We must also ensure that they have sufficient support, especially during times of calamity and severe drought.)

According to Pangilinan, the DAR is implementing solar-powered irrigation projects in partnership with the National Irrigation Administration (NIA) to ensure a more reliable water supply amid the El Niño.
He said the agency is also endorsing the use of El Niño-resilient crops and is offering climate-resilient farm productivity support to help increase yields and improve household incomes of the ARBs.
The senator said these projects are expected to benefit 579 communities, 734 agrarian reform beneficiary organizations (ARBOs), and 26,900 ARBs.

Of the P949 million allocated for the two programs, Pangilinan said P219 million is proposed for the Sustainable Livelihood Support for Disaster Areas, while P730 million would go to the Major Crop Farm Productivity Enhancement.
He said both programs aim to provide extension services, farm inputs, farm machinery, among others, to assist agrarian reform beneficiaries. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Mandarin Oriental is reborn, 12 years and a pandemic later
articles.summary: The 275-room luxury hotel reopens its doors just across the street from its old home, this time as part of the Ayala Triangle development

blocks.text: Composite by Guia Abogado/Rappler; Ayala Land photos
The 275-room luxury hotel reopens its doors just across the street from its old home, this time as part of the Ayala Triangle development

items: The new Mandarin Oriental hotel in Ayala Triangle, Makati, officially opened on November 26, 2020, after delays due to the pandemic, fulfilling a promise made in 2014.
The new hotel, designed by Skidmore, Owings & Merrill in collaboration with Leandro V. Locsin Partners, features 275 rooms, significantly fewer than the original hotel's 413 rooms.
Ayala Land aims to position the Philippines as a luxury tourism destination by emphasizing Filipino culture and craftsmanship in the hotel's design, rather than imitating other Asian luxury markets.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – When the last guests checked out of the Mandarin Oriental in September 2014, the hotel promised to be back in six years.
Makati would have to wait twice as long – with a pandemic in between that set back its original 2020 opening date – but the day has finally arrived.
On Thursday, November 26, Ayala Land opens the new Mandarin Oriental at Ayala Triangle, making good on a promise made more than a decade ago.

The original Mandarin opened on Makati Avenue in 1976, just in time for the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. Designed by National Artist for Architecture Leandro Locsin, it was among the first Mandarin Oriental hotels outside Hong Kong, arriving at a time when Makati was not yet the skyscraper-lined business district it is today.

That iconic structure has since been demolished, and in its place rises Park Central Towers, another Ayala Land development, billed as an ultra-luxury residential twin tower. (READ: Luxury condo resilience: Half of Ayala’s Laurean buyers staying despite pause)

Still, its successor, built just across the street, keeps a connection to the old Mandarin. American architectural firm Skidmore, Owings & Merrill designed the new hotel in collaboration with Leandro V. Locsin Partners, the practice founded by the late architect.

blocks.caption: REINVENTION. The 275-room Mandarin Hotel in Ayala Triangle, Makati City is owned by Ayala Land Hospitality and managed by Mandarin Oriental Hotel Group. Ayala Land handout

blocks.text: The new Mandarin is considerably smaller, at 275 rooms compared with its predecessor’s 413. That was part of the plan from the beginning, when Ayala Land first announced the project in June 2014.

The return of the Mandarin is also part of Ayala Land’s continuing reinvention of Ayala Triangle. Once part of Nielson Airport, the property went on to first house the Makati Stock Exchange and has today evolved into a hub anchored by Ayala Triangle Gardens Towers, with upscale restaurants and landscaped gardens – and finally, a luxury hotel to round it all out.

With the Mandarin, Ayala Land is also making a wager on the Philippines’ place in Asia’s luxury tourism market. The company believes Filipino culture and creativity can be a selling point in their own right, rather than looking to Singapore, Hong Kong, or Bangkok for a blueprint.

Filipino art, craftsmanship, and design feature prominently throughout the property. Ayala Land said it was designed around the idea that “the Philippines need not imitate other luxury destinations to compete with them.”

In the first nine months of 2026, Ayala Land’s leasing and hospitality revenues grew 8% year-on-year to P37.8 billion. Recurring-income businesses also now account for a greater part of the company’s earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA), standing at 55% and up from 44% in the same period last year. – Rappler.com

blocks.caption: Welcome to the ‘United States of Makati,’ where family income is PH’s highest – and most unequal
The renovation is done. Now Ayala is changing the shops inside its malls.

articles.title: ‘Pretty low’: Calgary girls' hockey team out $2,000 after tournament scam
articles.summary: A Calgary U-11 girls' hockey team lost nearly $2,000 — and the opportunity to play a tournament they thought they were accepted to — after falling victim to a scam. Last month, Hockey Alberta issued…

image.caption: Coach Dave Wilder says the team will add more checks and balances after falling victim to a tournament scam. (Submitted by Dave Wilder)

blocks.text: Calgary

A Calgary U-11 girls' hockey team lost nearly $2,000 — and the opportunity to play a tournament they thought they were accepted to — after falling victim to a scam. Last month, Hockey Alberta issued a warning on social media that it’s seeing a growing number of spoofed emails requesting money for tournaments.
Hockey Alberta warned last month it's seeing more of these scams
A Calgary U-11 girls’ hockey team lost nearly $2,000 — and the opportunity to play a tournament they thought they were accepted to — after falling victim to a scam.
Coach Dave Wilder says team volunteers applied to a tournament listed on Hockey Alberta's website slated to be held in Red Deer, Alta., in February.

They got an email saying they were admitted to the tournament, though it came from a different email address than the one listed on Hockey Alberta's website. At the time, Wilder says they didn’t think too much of it — teams and tournaments regularly create specific email addresses.
The email asked for $1,950, which they paid. It was only when they got another email asking for a deposit of $900 that the team got suspicious and started digging into it further.

That’s when they found out the girls actually hadn’t been accepted to the tournament, and scammers had made off with the money. The team filed a police report and is waiting to hear back if Scotiabank will reimburse them.
“Stealing money from little kids is a pretty low low,” Wilder said. “I'm not sure how it'll work out in the future, but there will definitely be more steps of due diligence involved.”
Scams on the rise

Last month, Hockey Alberta issued a warning on social media that it’s seeing a growing number of spoofed emails requesting money for tournaments. Teams across the country have posted similar warnings.
The Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre calls it spear phishing, and says it’s on the rise.

“In these types of fraud, criminals often take the time to research their intended targets,” the centre said in a statement, using social media, tournament schedules and hockey association websites to their advantage.

“Fraudsters understand that hockey teams regularly register for tournaments, pay registration fees and operate under deadlines. They take advantage of these routine activities, established relationships and the trust that exists within these communities.”

There were $87 million in losses from spear phishing in the first nine months of this year, a nearly 28-per-cent increase compared to all of 2025, the centre said. It also believes many frauds go unreported.
To protect themselves, the fraud centre recommends teams independently verify all payment requests and contact tournament owners directly.
Going forward

As for why more scammers might be targeting hockey teams, Wilder says it could be a case of supply and demand. Ice time is limited, as is tournament space, and scammers likely know teams might be eager to jump on any opportunity.
“I don't know if I'll let any of this ever slip through my hands again. I might have to drive to Red Deer to verify these people exist,” said Wilder.
The team has told parents about the scam, but so far not the girls. Wilder’s not sure they’ll be able to find another tournament to play in, and might instead schedule some exhibition games.
Parents were frustrated, he said, but still willing to pitch in. The team plans to find ways to fundraise to make up the missing funds.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jennifer is a reporter with CBC Calgary. Previously, she worked for CTV News in Toronto. You can reach her at jennifer.keiller@cbc.ca

articles.title: UK embassy in Japan warns of rise in drink spiking and credit card fraud at Tokyo bars
articles.summary:
Social media campaign fronted by British rapper Shao Dow advises tourists not to let their guard down

The British embassy in Tokyo has launched a social media campaign warning visitors to…

blocks.text: The British embassy in Tokyo has launched a social media campaign warning visitors to exercise caution after a rise in cases of drink-spiking and credit card fraud against tourists in the Japanese capital.

In a recent clip made in conjunction with the embassy, the British rapper and manga artist Shao Dow, a frequent visitor to Japan, notes that although the country “is incredibly safe, that doesn’t mean you can let your guard down”.

He warns that young male tourists are particularly susceptible to being lured into bars on the promise of being able to chat to attractive, English-speaking women. They are then served drug-laced drinks and enormous sums are charged to their credit cards.
Drink-spiking cases involving British and other international tourists have been on the rise in the past two years in popular nightlife districts such as Roppongi, Shibuya and Kabukicho.

Some victims have lost up to £30,000 (US$39,000) in a single night, Dow says, and wake up with no memory of what happened. “Look, do me a favour,” he adds, “Stay alert, trust your gut, keep an eye on your stuff and don’t follow strangers into bars.”

Police in Tokyo have come under pressure to tackle the rise in incidents targeting tourists. Earlier this month, 160 riot police conducted predawn raids on two establishments in Kabukicho after reports they had ripped off customers. Five people were arrested.

Between January and October, police recorded 340 cases – up 195 from last year – in the Shinjuku area after customers, some of whom were lured into bars by street touts, were charged extortionate sums. In one case, ¥9.6m ($60,000) was allegedly charged to a customer’s credit card.

According to the newspaper Asahi Shimbun, victims have paid ¥390m in total and foreign nationals had been the targets in 70% of cases. The newspaper quoted a senior investigator as saying the reported crimes were the “tip of the iceberg” since many visitors returned home before they realised they had been swindled, while others had left Japan without reporting the incidents to police.
Reports say the rise in cases was being fuelled by Japan’s tourism boom. A record 42.7 million people visited Japan last year, including 530,000 from the UK.

articles.title: Spain: Catalan separatist Puigdemont sets date for return
articles.summary: Former Catalan leader Carles Puigdemont plans to return to Barcelona on December 12 after nearly a decade in exile. Spain's Supreme Court has dropped the criminal case against him, clearing the way…

image.caption: Spain's Supreme Court has cleared Puigdemont to return, nearly a decade after Catalonia's failed bid for independence [FILE: October 27, 2025]Image: Glòria Sánchez/Europa Press/IMAGO

blocks.text: Catalan separatist leader Carles Puigdemont said he would return to Spain on December 12, nearly a decade after fleeing the country following a failed independence bid.
The announcement comes just days after Spain's Supreme Court closed criminal proceedings against him under a controversial amnesty law, removing the last legal obstacle to his return.
Speaking at a televised news conference in Brussels, Puigdemont said he would return to the Catalan parliament in Barcelona.

"I left as President of the Government of Catalonia, and I will return to the place where Catalan democracy elects or dismisses its presidents: the Parliament of Catalonia. I will do so on Saturday, 12 December, at midday, and that very night I will be able to sleep at home, with my family," he said.
Puigdemont also announced plans to present a proposal for a renewed push for independence of Catalonia on December 17.
Who is Carles Puigdemont?
Puigdemont is a former president of Catalonia, a wealthy region in northeastern Spain with its own language, culture and a strong independence movement.
He led Catalonia's regional government in October 2017 when it organized a referendum on independence from Spain that Spanish courts had declared illegal.

The vote and the subsequent failed attempt to break away from Spain triggered the country's worst political crisis in decades, deepening tensions between the central government in Madrid and Catalan separatists.

blocks.caption: Thousands of Catalan independence supporters gathered in Barcelona in September 2017, weeks before the disputed independence referendum [FILE: September 11, 2017]Image: Reuters/S. Vera

blocks.text: Puigdemont fled to Belgium that same month to avoid arrest and has lived in self-imposed exile ever since.

His "Junts per Catalunya" party remains an important force in Spanish politics and played a key role in securing the parliamentary support needed for Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez to remain in power in 2023.
Why has Puigdemont now been cleared to return to Spain?
Spain's Supreme Court on Monday shelved the criminal case against Puigdemont after applying an amnesty law passed by parliament in 2024.
In a ruling dated November 20, the court determined that the amnesty had extinguished any potential criminal liability for Puigdemont and two other separatist figures.

blocks.caption: Puigdemont briefly returned to Barcelona in August 2024 to address supporters before leaving again without being arrested, despite an outstanding arrest warrant [FILE: August 8, 2024]Image: Manaure Quintero/AFP

blocks.text: The decision followed a Constitutional Court ruling in October that extended the amnesty to cover embezzlement allegations linked to Catalonia's independence bid.
The Supreme Court had initially ruled that the law did not apply to those investigated for embezzlement, including Puigdemont.

Following the Constitutional Court's intervention, the Supreme Court lifted the arrest warrant against him. Monday's decision to close the criminal proceedings completed the legal process, allowing him to return without facing detention over the 2017 case.
Why is Spain's Catalan amnesty law controversial?
The amnesty was a key concession by Sanchez to Catalan separatist parties, including Puigdemont's Junts, in exchange for their support following Spain's inconclusive 2023 general election.

The agreement allowed Sanchez to secure another term as prime minister but sparked strong opposition from conservative parties and critics who accused him of putting his political survival ahead of Spain's interests.

blocks.caption: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez secured the support of Catalan separatist parties in 2023 in exchange for an amnesty law [FILE: October 16, 2026]Image: Stephanie Lecocq/REUTERS

blocks.text: The conservative Popular Party (PP) and far-right Vox opposed the legislation and unsuccessfully challenged it in parliament and the courts.
The controversy intensified after Puigdemont said in a recent interview with Spanish newspaper El Mundo that his party had exploited Sanchez's ambition to secure concessions for Catalonia.
"We had to test how far we could go," Puigdemont said, calling Sanchez "an amoral person with an excessive thirst for power".
"We have exploited this excessive ambition for power to inflict certain defeats on Spain that we would otherwise not have been able to bring about."

blocks.caption: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez (front row, left) applauds as parliament approves a controversial amnesty law for Catalan separatists [FILE: May 30, 2024]Image: Bernat Armangue/AP/picture alliance

blocks.text: His remarks became a flashpoint in the campaign ahead of Spain's snap general election on November 29.
Polls suggest the Popular Party is likely to win the most seats but fall short of an outright majority, potentially leaving it dependent on Vox to form a government.

articles.title: House leaders: VP Sara's survey scores not a pass for unexplained wealth
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte's high ratings in opinion surveys do not give her a pass on the alleged unexplained wealth for which she has been impeached, House leaders said Wednesday.

blocks.text: Published November 25, 2026 7:50pm
Vice President Sara Duterte's high ratings in opinion surveys do not give her a pass on the alleged unexplained wealth for which she has been impeached, House leaders said Wednesday.

“The point here is accountability. The impeachment trial is not based on fame, popularity in social media, or ranking in surveys. The impeachment trial is based on documents presented to support or dispute the allegations,” House Deputy Speaker Janet Garin of Iloilo said in a press conference.

“These allegations need to be addressed. No survey can erase the accountability of any high-ranking official, at naniniwala kami base sa historical data at experience natin [and we believe that based on historical data and our own experience], the Senator-judges will decide based on the documents presented, not popularity,” she added.

The answer was in response to a question about polls showing the Vice President as the frontrunner in the 2028 presidential election—an election that no one else has yet announced their intention to run for, and which she may not be eligible for if the impeachment court convicts her.

At the impeachment trial, an expert witness for the prosecution testified that Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, accumulated unexplained wealth of at least P817 million to as much as P1.5 billion.
House Deputy Speaker Jefferson Khonghun of Zambales Khonghun agreed that the impeachment process is not a popularity contest.
“The impeachment process requires transparency, accountability, especially about her wealth,” he said.
“Hindi naman tayo kinakabahan dahil hindi issue dito kung ikaw sikat o popular. Ang issue dito, ipaliwanag mo ‘yung yaman [mo]. Saan galing ang pera,” headded.
(We're not worried [about the trial outcome] because the issue here is not whether you are famous or popular. The issue is the [unexplained] wealth. Where did the money come from?)

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero earlier pointed out that even if the declared assets of the Vice President and her husband in their joint Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN) from 2022 to 2025 are added up—meaning they did not spend in that period—their total declared net worth of P336 million would still be way lower than the P424 million in bank transactions recorded under the bank accounts of the Duterte-Carpio couple from 2022 to 2025 based on the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) records.

Moreover, Escudero said that the that the total net worth of the Duterte-Carpio couple at P840 million as declared in their joint SALN from 2007 to 2025 is also by a mile lower than the P4.4 billion worth of bank transactions recorded under the spouses’ bank accounts from 2007 to 2025, also based from AMLC records.
The defense is yet to present a witness that disputes the P4.4 billion of bank transactions recorded under the bank accounts of the Duterte-Carpio couple.
The defense already presented at least nine witnesses so far but nobody of them disputed that P4.4 billion of bank transactions were recorded under the accounts of the Duterte-Carpio couple.
But in a television interview aired on Monday, the Vice President maintained that she is not in the wrong, considering that she has the majority of the people’s support.
Khonghun, however, responded that earning sympathy does not dispute allegations.
“She has the right to seek sympathy of the people, but again, such cannot erase the documents that has been presented by the prosecution,” he said.

“History will judge a public official on how they responded to the allegations. Kung malinis ang ating konsiyensiya, harapin at sagutin niya ang mga katanungan. Ganun lang ka simple ‘yun,” Khonghun added.
(If her conscience is clear, she should be able to face the questions and answer them. It's that simple.) — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Philippines’ biggest HiFi exhibit set this weekend
articles.summary: Admission is free for all audio and music lovers, and there's no need to pre-register

blocks.text: Admission is free for all audio and music lovers, and there's no need to pre-register
(This is a press release from the November HiFi Show organizers.)
A team of Filipino audio experts is holding a HiFi show this weekend in Makati City.
The November HiFi Show is the Philippines’ biggest hi-fi exhibition, the country’s premier gathering for music lovers and audio enthusiasts that has been around for 24 years.
Each year, it brings together leading and local international brands showcasing the finest in high-fidelity and high-quality sound systems, speakers, amplifiers, turntables, and more.

Beyond the gear, it’s also a treasure trove for collectors, with rare finds, vinyl records, and CDs waiting to be discovered. More than just an exhibition, the November HiFi Show is a celebration of sound culture — where innovation, passion, and community converge.

“Since 2008, my team of Filipino audio experts and I have been doing this purely for the love of the hobby—no commercial agenda, just a shared mission to build world-class, 100% Filipino-made DIY high-end audio gear,” said veteran business journalist and Rappler columnist Val Villanueva.
The November HiFi Show 2026 will be held on November 28 to 29 at the Makati Diamond Residences, 118 Legazpi Street, Legazpi Village, Makati City.
Parking can be found nearby Greenbelt Malls, and street side parking is available in Legazpi Village.

articles.title: Trump says pardon for Nvidia boss Huang ‘always an option’ after accusations of breaking export laws – US politics live
articles.summary: The US president urged the tech leader to ‘tell the truth’ in upcoming testimony in a Senate hearing

blocks.text: Trump considering pardon for Huang after Nvidia CEO accused of breaking export control laws
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump has said he would consider pardoning Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, if necessary, but added that he did not think it would come to that.

Chuck Schumer, the current Senate minority leader vying to lead the Democratic majority in the next Congress, yesterday accused Huang of shipping “extremely advanced chips to China” and violating US export control laws.
Schumer said the move “amounts to the equivalent of selling rocket engines to the Soviets during the space race”.
But in an interview with the the New York Post, the president – took credit for convincing Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang - admitted he could intervene again to help the embattled CEO.
“It’s always an option, I guess, but I don’t think it’ll be necessary,” the president told the rightwing tabloid owned by his supporter, Rupert Murdoch.

Asked about Huang’s upcoming testimony to a US Senate banking committee hearing on export controls, Trump said that he sees no reason for the chief executive, who admitted an affair to a Chinese woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence, to invoke his Fifth amendment right to avoid answering questions that might incriminate him.

“I don’t think he needs to take the Fifth. I think it’s an interesting story for people,” Trump said. “I think I want him to just tell the truth, and I mean, his lawyers are going to have to advise him, but I’ve always found him to be 100% aboveboard, and you know a very smart person.”

Nvidia’s board reinstated Huang on Monday after Donald Trump says he intervened on the executive’s behalf, assuring company leadership that he did not pose a national security risk despite questions surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, a tech executive of no relation who has been accused of acting as a Chinese asset and routing advanced chips to Beijing via her datacenter company, Megaspeed.
In other developments:

items: Trump also told the New York Post that he would meet with senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat he repeatedly lied about on the campaign trail last month, when he referred to the Muslim physician as “a jihadist”. “He’s a smart guy,” Trump told the tabloid’s reporters.

Kilmar Ábrego Garcia voluntarily left the United States on a flight for Spain on Tuesday night, bringing an end to the 20-month legal battle that followed his wrongful deportation to El Salvador, in violation of a court order.

articles.title: From 'Super' to 'Godzilla' to 'Mega': Just how monstrous is this year's El Niño?

image.caption: Powerful waves generated by a very strong El Niño crash into seaside homes at Mondos Beach in California in January 2016. Scientists say the El Niño developing in 2026 could be even stronger, potentially ranking among the most powerful on record. (Mark Ralston/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Godzilla has battled giant moths and three-headed dragons. But even the king of the kaiju might have trouble keeping up with this year's El Niño.
First came "Super El Niño." Then "Godzilla El Niño." Now there's a new monster in town: "Mega El Niño." At this rate, King Ghidorah may be next.
But has this year's El Niño really been upgraded?

"As far as I can tell there's no reason to invent a new category above 'very strong' that we have right now," said Emily Becker, a research associate professor of atmospheric sciences at the University of Miami's Rosenstiel School.
But David Phillips, a climatologist emeritus with Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC), was more enthusiastic, given the unprecedented nature of this El Niño.
"Maybe 'Godzilla' is not strong enough for it."

A NASA visualization compares Pacific Ocean surface temperatures in 2025 and 2026, showing the dramatic warming associated with El Niño. Red indicates warmer-than-average water, while blue shows cooler-than-average temperatures. The maps use satellite-derived data averaged over seven days to highlight broader temperature patterns. (NASA/JPL)
What's behind the 'mega' headlines?

El Niño is a climate phenomenon that occurs when unusually warm water in the central and eastern tropical Pacific alters atmospheric circulation patterns, changing the weather around the world, according to ECCC.

Scientists measure the strength of an El Niño by averaging the sea surface temperature over three months in a large section of the Pacific Ocean, as opposed to measuring extreme temperatures in localized areas.

The latest name gained attention after U.S. meteorologist Ryan Maue posted a map on X on Sunday showing what he said were sea surface temperatures as much as 10 C above normal near Peru and the Galápagos Islands.
"This is now a Mega El Niño," he wrote.
+10°C sea surface temperature anomaly near Galapagos 🐢and off coast of Peru. This is now a Mega El Niño. https://t.co/xfavOfY16L—RyanWeather

But the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)'s analysis doesn't show temperatures that high at the ocean's surface, said Michelle L'Heureux, its El Niño team lead and a physical scientist with the U.S. National Weather Service.
Instead, it shows temperature anomalies of roughly 4 C to 6 C in the eastern Pacific, she said.
NOAA hasn't changed its terminology for classifying El Niño events, said meteorologist Erica Cei, a National Weather Service spokesperson.
The agency's Climate Prediction Center simply classifies El Niño events as weak, moderate, strong or very strong.

NOAA's Nov. 12 update reported extremely high sea surface temperatures in parts of the eastern Pacific. However, isolated temperature readings do not necessarily reflect the overall intensity of an El Niño.

items: Will this year’s super El Niño push 2026 to be the warmest year on record?

blocks.text: Instead, NOAA uses the Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI) to measure average sea surface temperature anomalies in the central tropical Pacific over a three-month period, while accounting for warming across other tropical oceans. By that measure, this year's El Niño has reached NOAA's highest classification: very strong.
"This event is running on par with our previous very strong events," Becker said, referring to the El Niños of 1997-'98 and 2015-'16.

While "mega El Niño" is not an official category, the term has appeared in the scientific literature. A 2023 peer-reviewed study used it to describe the very strong El Niño events of 1982-'83, 1997-'98 and 2015-'16.
I’ve tracked El Niño for years — I’ve never seen this before
Is this El Niño really exceptional?
There is no question this is an unusually powerful event.
NOAA's Nov. 12 forecast gave it roughly a 60 per cent chance of surpassing the strength of previous El Niños dating back to 1950.
But that remains a forecast, not a record already broken.
Mandy Freund, a climate science lecturer at the University of Melbourne who has written about "Godzilla El Niño," said some ocean temperatures recorded near South America are unprecedented.

items: This year will be a super-duper El Niño. Here's what Canadians can expect this winter

blocks.text: She also defended the dramatic terminology.
"I believe if the language serves the purpose of raising awareness of a dangerous situation, that’s acceptable," she said in an email to CBC News.
But Freund said making bold predictions before forecasts become reliable could undermine public confidence.
Becker also cautioned against assuming that an exceptionally strong El Niño will always bring extreme weather: "We don't necessarily expect to see extreme impacts from an extreme El Niño."

A skier walks down a patchy ski slope at Whistler, B.C., in December 2023. A powerful El Niño is expected to bring warmer-than-normal temperatures to much of Canada this winter, potentially affecting snowfall and conditions at ski resorts. (Ethan Cairns/The Canadian Press)
What could a very strong El Niño mean for Canada?
Western and central Canada typically experience a milder winter during El Niño years, but impacts can be quite variable.
ECCC's Nov. 1 seasonal forecast also suggests that much of Eastern Canada could experience above-normal temperatures this winter.
Phillips said the current season could be compared with the very mild winter Canada experienced in 2023-'24. But even with very strong El Niño conditions, cold spells and snowstorms are possible.

items: How could El Niño affect Ontario's winter?

blocks.text: An area of great uncertainty this winter is the polar vortex, a large circulation of winds in the upper atmosphere over the Arctic. When it is disrupted and weakens, cold Arctic air can push down into Canada and the United States.
Phillips compared this coming winter to a clash straight out of a Hollywood blockbuster: "It's the Godzilla El Niño meeting the frigid polar vortex," he said.
The lack of winter snow and moisture could increase the risk of spring drought and lead to an earlier start to the wildfire season, Phillips said.
The Kelvin wave along B.C. may be 'strongest El Niño we've ever seen’ | Hanomansing Live
Is climate change making El Niños more powerful?
It is still unclear whether human-caused climate change is making powerful El Niños more frequent or intense.

Canada's Changing Climate Report 2026 finds, with medium confidence, that year-to-year climate fluctuations associated with El Niño have been larger since 1950 than in the previous century, but expresses low confidence that the change is due to human activity. This is because El Niño itself is highly variable, making it difficult to separate natural fluctuations from the effects of climate change.
There is no evidence to suggest that exceptionally powerful El Niños are increasing in frequency, Becker said.

items: Why is it so warm in Canada's north right now?

blocks.text: However, global warming can make the effects of a strong El Niño even worse because warmer air holds more moisture and can cause more rainfall in regions that are already wet during an El Niño year.
Phillips called the combination of a powerful El Niño and a warming planet a "double whammy."
So while there is no official classification for a "mega" El Niño, the El Niño monster is out there somewhere.

articles.title: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
articles.summary:
Kishanth Peramalya was denied entry due to sexual assault convictions and sent to Africa where he had no connections

The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual…

blocks.text: The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.

Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.

In November 2024, the UK allowed 61 migrants to enter from Diego Garcia after a damning UN report about conditions in the camp. However, the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, denied Peramalya entry to the UK due to his criminal convictions while he was on Diego Garcia for four counts of sexual assault, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of arson. Cooper’s decision was upheld by UK courts.

Peramalya had been granted protection from being returned to Sri Lanka, having been tortured and sexually abused by Sri Lankan military personnel as a teenager. In late March, the Maldives said it would take him for 30 days, according to the BBC. He was then transferred to Eswatini, a country landlocked by South Africa and Mozambique and formerly known as Swaziland, where he killed himself on 13 September.

A draft deal between the UK and Eswatini governments would have committed Downing Street to cover the costs of Peramalya’s resettlement there for three years, according to the BBC, which said the UK was also finalising arrangements for Peramalya to live in Eswatini permanently.

The Guardian has not seen the draft deal. Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, said: “The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances.”

She said that no formal agreement was ever reached over Peramalya’s long-term residency status with the UK and declined to comment further on the specific arrangements of his stay in Eswatini or the circumstances around his death.

Mdluli said: “Eswatini has not received any other similar request from the government of the United Kingdom. The government of the Kingdom of Eswatini remains committed to ensuring that any agreements entered into with external partners safeguard national interest as well as the safety and security of Emaswati [Swazi people].”

A UK government spokesperson said: “Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK. We continue to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case.”
Peramalya had post-traumatic stress disorder and attempted suicide multiple times on Diego Garcia, according to a UK high court judgment in February 2025.

Peramalya’s family told the BBC he was initially housed alone in an isolated guesthouse in Eswatini. “My brother did not want to go there at all,” said his sister, speaking from India. “He couldn’t manage being there alone, he was very lonely.”
after newsletter promotion

She said he had called her four times a day and was initially having weekly psychiatric appointments, which were made daily when his mental health deteriorated, as well as having someone brought in to prepare his food.
Peramalya’s relatives said they were not aware of his convictions for sexual offences or any plan to make his transfer to Eswatini permanent.

Eswatini has accepted dozens of third-country deportees from the US since July 2025. In November 2025, its government confirmed it had received $5.1m in exchange for taking up to 160 migrants from the US.

articles.title: Indian Cockroach movement leader asks court for permission to fly to UK
articles.summary:
Officials at Delhi airport stopped Saurav Das from boarding flight to Britain, where students have invited him to speak

A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has asked the Delhi…

blocks.text: A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has asked the Delhi high court to give him permission to fly to the UK after immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him boarding a flight early on Tuesday morning.

The court is scheduled to hear Saurav Das’s case on Thursday morning. His lawyer asked the court for a quick hearing because Das has by now already missed some of his engagements at British universities and can only attend the other events on his itinerary if he is allowed to fly out as soon as possible.
Das, 27, is one of the main faces of the Cockroach movement, which shot into the political firmament out of nowhere in May to challenge the Narendra Modi government with street protests.
The movement succeeded in forcing the education minister to resign in July over exam leaks and has since functioned as a pressure group.
Das had been invited by the Oxford Union Society to participate in a “fireside chat” on the movement.
Indian student groups at Edinburgh, Cambridge, Queen Mary University of London and the London School of Economics have also invited him to speak.
“Students want to know how we succeeded without any violence, how we began and where we are going. There is a great curiosity about the movement,” Das told the Guardian.
Reports in the Indian media have alleged that Das was informed well before the flight that his passport contained discrepancies.

“None of these reports is true,” said Das. “I received an email five hours before my flight saying that I should not use my passport for travel. It gave no reason. And I did not see the email until I arrived at Delhi airport. What’s more, I’ve travelled abroad before on this passport since it was issued in 2019 so what’s the problem with it now?”

He suspects that the government is using a frivolous case filed in Chennai against him as a pretext. The case has been filed, Das surmises, by someone hostile to the Cockroach movement and disputes his citizenship.

Das believes he was deliberately stopped by a government that is “scared” of someone such as him speaking abroad about the ideals of Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru (independent India’s first prime minister) and that it wanted to make an example of him.
“It’s a chilling signal to young Indians that we can do what we like, that if we can do this to a leader of a movement, we can do this to you too,” said Das.
after newsletter promotion
In recent years, the government has stopped foreign speakers and academics, including several from the UK, from entering India.

Last year, Francesca Orsini, a professor at Soas University of London, was stopped at Delhi airport and deported despite holding a valid visa. The government said she had been blacklisted for allegedly conducting research and speaking at events while visiting on a tourist visa in 2024.
Also last year, Nitasha Kaul, a professor at Westminster University, was detained at Bangalore airport and deported for “anti-India activities”.

Some people who find themselves blacklisted have chosen to fight back. In 2023, the UK-based journalist Amrit Wilson had her overseas citizen of India card which allows free movement into India cancelled, also for alleged “anti-India activities”.
She took legal action and earlier this week, the Delhi high court ruled that the government had failed to give any concrete details of what it meant by “anti-India activities”.
The court has given the government a week to issue a fresh notice, this time giving specific reasons.

articles.title: North Korea expels Swiss envoy over sanctions on camp accused of indoctrinating Ukrainian children
articles.summary: North Korea has ordered Switzerland to close its newly reopened diplomatic office. The dispute centers on Swiss sanctions against a camp accused of indoctrinating Ukrainian children from…

image.caption: Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis met his North Korean counterpart, Choe Son Hui, in Pyongyang in October to discuss normalizing diplomatic relations [FILE: October 30, 2026]Image: KCNA/KNS/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: North Korea has declared Switzerland's top diplomatic representative in Pyongyang persona non grata and ordered him to leave the country within 48 hours, state media reported on Wednesday.

The North Korean Foreign Ministry also called for the closure of Switzerland's diplomatic office in the capital, less than a month after it reopened following a lengthy shutdown during the COVID-19 pandemic.

blocks.caption: Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis met with senior North Korean ruling party official Jo Yong Won during his visit to Pyongyang in October [FILE: October 30, 2026]Image: KCNA/KNS/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to the state-run Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), Pak Hyon Su, director general of the ministry's European Department, summoned Swiss diplomat Sylvain Astier and handed him a memorandum demanding the office's closure.
Pyongyang said the decision was in response to Switzerland's sanctions against a North Korean children's camp, describing the move as an openly hostile act.
"Any act of violating the sovereign rights of the DPRK and the interests of its citizens can never be welcomed by us," KCNA reported, using the acronym for North Korea's official name.
Why did Switzerland impose sanctions on North Korea?
Switzerland placed the Songdowon International Children's Camp in the coastal city of Wonsan under sanctions on November 4.

Swiss authorities accused the camp, which also hosts Chinese and Russian students, of participating in the "transfer of Ukrainian children from temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine" to North Korea.
They also said the facility contributed to "efforts aimed at the ideological conditioning and russification of Ukrainian children".

blocks.caption: Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, condemned the Swiss sanctions [FILE: August 10, 2022]Image: Korean Central News Agency/Korea News Service/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: On Tuesday, Kim Yo Jong, the influential sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, condemned the sanctions arguing that the measures violated North Korea's sovereignty by interfering with its responsibility to provide children with cultural and recreational opportunities.
How has Switzerland responded to North Korea's decision?
Switzerland's Foreign Ministry said on Tuesday that reopening its diplomatic office was independent of its sanctions policy.

"The reopening of the Swiss diplomatic office in Pyongyang is in line with our universalist foreign policy. Its aim is to maintain channels of dialogue, including with states with which we have differences on certain issues," the ministry said.
It stressed that this approach applied regardless of Switzerland's participation in UN sanctions over North Korea's nuclear program or EU sanctions related to Russia's war against Ukraine.
Swiss authorities were not immediately available for further comment on Wednesday.
South Korea proposes talks to officially end war with North
Switzerland has maintained diplomatic relations with North Korea since 1974 and has long served as an intermediary between Pyongyang and Western countries.

Its office in the North Korean capital closed during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis formally reopened it during a visit in October, when he discussed normalizing relations.
It was the first visit by a Swiss government minister to North Korea since 2003.
The office operates under the Swiss Embassy in Beijing, which handles diplomatic and consular relations with North Korea. Pyongyang also maintains an embassy in Bern.
Only a few European countries have diplomatic missions in North Korea, including Sweden, Poland and the Czech Republic.
What does North Korea's move mean for relations with the West?
Experts say the expulsion is intended as a warning to other Western countries, including the United States, which has been seeking to reestablish contact with Pyongyang.
"North Korea is using Switzerland as a test case to show that sanctions and dialogue are incompatible," Lim Eul-chul, a professor at South Korea's Kyungnam University, told news agency Reuters.

blocks.caption: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has expressed a willingness to expand diplomatic ties with countries that respect North Korea's sovereignty [FILE: October 23, 2026]Image: KCNA/KNS/AFP

blocks.text: Ahn Chan-il, a researcher originally from North Korea, told agency AFP that Pyongyang, backed by its allies China and Russia, wanted to make an example of Switzerland.
Earlier this week, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un personally received credentials from the new ambassadors of 10 countries, including Russia and Sweden, in a rare diplomatic ceremony.
Kim said Pyongyang was seeking to expand relations with countries that respected its sovereignty but would oppose attempts to restrict the rights and development of sovereign states.

articles.title: China misusing Interpol to target dissidents, says leading UK lawyer
articles.summary:
Concerns over Beijing’s use of ‘red notices’ as Hong Kong prepares to host police organisation’s general assembly

China is misusing Interpol to target and silence dissidents, a leading…

blocks.text: China is misusing Interpol to target and silence dissidents, a leading British lawyer has claimed, as Hong Kong prepares to host the police organisation’s general assembly for the first time.

Ben Keith, a specialist in “red notices” - the Interpol system under which national authorities are requested to locate and detain suspects - said he was working on five cases involving China making questionable requests through Interpol.

He revealed that he had also contacted officials at the law enforcement organisation in July on behalf of a group of five high-profile UK-based Chinese dissidents to find out if Beijing had sought the issuance of red notices relating to them.

Interpol responded in October that they were looking into his request for information but there had been no substantive information shared, he added, raising concerns that there might be data relating to the individuals on the Interpol system.

He said: “If there’s no data, than they will tell me there’s no data. If there is data, then they have to get permission from Hong Kong to tell me. It has been sometime now. Given the profile of these individuals, I think they may have had some data on them. That’s the fear.”

Many Hong Kong democracy campaigners who fled to the UK in recent years have British national (overseas) status but this does not protect them from red notices outside the UK and potential extradition to China.

A red notice is a request to law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender, or similar legal action. It is based on an arrest warrant or court order issued by the judicial authorities in the requesting country. Member countries apply their own laws in deciding whether to arrest a person.

Keith said: “The Russian playbook was to accuse political opponents or business opponents of some sort of really technical criminal offence of fraud, employment law breach, regulatory offence, that sort of thing, to disguise the real purpose of the request. The Chinese have taken that on.”

Hong Kong will host the 94th Interpol general assembly between 30 November and 3 December, attracting police chiefs from its 196 member countries to set global policing policy, approve budgets and activities, and pass binding resolutions.

Keith said that hosting the assembly offered an opportunity for China to “reputation wash”, arguing that Beijing ran a sophisticated public relations machine to hide the high proportion of red notice and extradition requests that were politically motivated.

The red notice system is used by China to target those sought under the state campaigns launched under President Xi Jinping to track down fugitives overseas and recover illicit funds, known as Operations Fox Hunt and Sky Net, it is claimed.

A new report, The Red Notice Trap, by Ben Keith and Rhys Davies of the legal firm IHR Advisors, draws on court judgments, Interpol records and Chinese-language official documents, to show how red notices fit into Beijing’s campaign to silence critics and bring them home for persecution.

It notes under a 2025 revision of the implementing regulations for the People’s Repubilc of China’s supervision law that red notice requests sit with extradition, judicial assistance, law enforcement cooperation, prosecution abroad, asset seizure and ‘ideological education’, as tools for the recovery of people.

blocks.caption: Yidiresi Aishan, AKA Idris Hassan, a Uyghur activist, was detained after a red notice was issued by Interpol at China’s request.  Photograph: AP

blocks.text: Among the cases cited in the IHR Advisors report is that of Yidiresi Aishan – a Uyghur activist who is also known as Idris Hassan – who was arrested in July 2021, when arriving at Casablanca airport on a flight from Turkey, where he had been living.

He was detained on the basis of a red notice issued by Interpol at China’s request “for belonging to a terrorist organisation”. Within two weeks, Interpol suspended the notice as it breached its rules and it was later cancelled.
The Moroccan extradition proceedings carried on regardless and in December 2021 the country’s court of cassation approved Hasan’s surrender to China.

The UN committee against torture found that Hasan’s extradition would breach article 3 of the convention against torture and Morocco did not carry out the extradition But Hasan remained in detention until 12 February 2025 after spending nearly four years in prison on the basis of an Interpol red notice.
“His case shows the central weakness this report returns to: Interpol can correct its own data, but it cannot undo what national authorities have already set in motion”, the authors write.
Hasan, who now lives in Canada, said he no longer travelled and that his life had been thrown “upside down”.
“Four years of life have gone, just spent in prison, I could not be with my children,” he told the Guardian. “Everything has changed. I cannot describe this. But I trust Canada.”
Hasan added: “I don’t understand how this kind of the big organisation like Interpol how they took my name down without evidence, without nothing. Just put my name out.”
Interpol and the Chinese embassy have been approached for comment.

articles.title: Pro-Palestine activist sought by US in extradition case: ‘I still have a right to my beliefs’
articles.summary:
James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, at center of legal fight, says he ‘should not be unjustly accused’ because of leftwing views

James “Fergie” Chambers, the wealthy leftwing activist and donor…

blocks.text: James “Fergie” Chambers, the wealthy leftwing activist and donor controversially sought in extradition by the US, has told the Guardian that he is “not asking anyone to endorse my ideas or not think I’m a jerk – but I still have a right to my beliefs and should not be unjustly accused because of them”.

Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.
The complaint also includes riot and conspiracy to riot charges stemming from 2023 protests against New England branches of Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit.

Chambers was speaking from his Madrid apartment in his first in-depth interview after a Spanish appeals court ordered his provisional release on bail on Friday. That release was due to issues with the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported by the Guardian.
“Support for my case doesn’t imply support of me, or my ideas,” Chambers said. “It’s about my right to have those ideas – and not be falsely accused of things.”
Chambers, whose case has gained attention across the world, had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza.

The order granting Chambers’s provisional release asserted that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”. Spanish judges had previously denied bail three times.

The wealthy heir to at least $250mn from his family’s business – Atlanta–based Cox Enterprises – was in the middle of his first visit without being separated by glass with his mother, Lauren Hamilton, when he was summoned to receive the “good news” on Friday, Chambers told the Guardian.

Minutes later, he returned to tell his mother he was being released. “She freaked out crying. We went nuts for about five minutes. Then we got to contacting my lawyer and getting my kids on a plane to Spain.”
On Monday, Chambers’s five-year-old son with actor and activist Stella Schnabel could be heard in the background. The tableau was in stark contrast to his months in prison.

“I tried to build a cocoon to deal with the immense unknown, the immense fear,” he said of his time in Aranjuez prison. “I would pray a lot. The only idea I could hold onto was, my home is the truth. The truth of who loves you. The truth of my own innocence. And the truth of what is happening in Palestine and all the things connected to what is happening in Palestine – other wars, gas prices. No one can take that away from you.”

blocks.caption: Stella Schnabel, Chambers’s wife, and lawyer Baltasar Garzon speak to the media in Madrid in September. Photograph: Eduardo Parra/Europa Press/Getty Images

blocks.text: Chambers has been supported by his mother throughout his case, and has reconnected with his father, James Cox Chambers – who owns an estimated 17% stake in Cox Enterprises but does not play an active role in the company – for the first time in five years.
“Speaking with my parents has provided emotional stability – and intelligent, adult minds to help make decisions,” Chambers said.

Although he has had political disagreements with his father, a donor to the Democratic party, Chambers said his father “sees this situation as totally unthinkable and out of step with anything resembling a just society”.
He also invoked his grandfather, the ACLU civil rights lawyer James Cox Hamilton, who died in 2014. “He would’ve turned in his grave over this,” Chambers said.

While locked up, Chambers, a US citizen, received hundreds of letters of support from friends, family and strangers, postmarked from Atlanta to Barcelona – including, he said, “from a guy who had been imprisoned under [Spanish dictator Francisco] Franco, who painted the ‘key of return’ [a symbol of homes lost in the 1948 Nakba] on the Palestinian flag”.

Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”
after newsletter promotion

His release followed a separate decision on Thursday by a three-judge panel at Spain’s high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish.

The US admitted to making several of the changes, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent”. These and dozens of other changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian last week.

It was also recently revealed that there is no indictment behind the complaint, meaning the federal government has not had a grand jury evaluate evidence against Chambers, and instead is seeking his extradition based on the affidavit of a single FBI agent, the core of the sealed criminal complaint.

During his time in prison, Chambers also began the process of applying for political asylum in Spain. He cannot be extradited until the asylum case runs its course, and also cannot be extradited if he is granted asylum. His legal team has notified the government office evaluating his asylum petition of the altered translations.

Chambers was arrested 10 July as he and Schnabel pulled into the driveway of a school they were visiting to see about enrolling their five-year-old, part of plans to move to Spain. They had been staying in Ireland, where Schnabel was working on a film.

Although the arrest came as a surprise – “I was confused! Did I speed?” he thought – Chambers revealed to the Guardian that a car had been following him around Dublin only days before, and that someone had broken into their car parked outside their house at night, without taking anything of value.
“I noticed signs of surveillance,” he said. Months later, last Wednesday, Irish police raided the same house, acting on a request from US authorities.
With his immediate future uncertain, Chambers said he was “looking forward to sharing a couple of nice dinners with my family this week”.
As for the past, he said the millions he has donated to an estimated 100 projects in about 20 countries is “the most important thing I’ve done”.

“Somebody with the political orientation I have and with resources, no matter how good of an activist I am, it’s not gonna be as effective as medical aid or feeding children in Gaza, supporting independent media that wouldn’t otherwise exist, or paying people’s bail who have been arrested for protesting.
“I’m giving a lot of money to things that other people aren’t giving money to.”
Chambers also said he was “grateful for the way Spanish courts have dealt with this – just focusing on the facts. It shouldn’t matter that I’ve made some emotional statements.”
